utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were reported. Mr. Groome, you received the outcome of the Chamber's response to your proposals, which [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And a further detail most likely will follow in the course of this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are. We would like to have on the stand, Mr. Lubura, Veljko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lubura. The usher will hand out you to the text of a solemn declaration. I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Lubura, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Lubura.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noticed, Your Honours, I'm just looking at the list, and I see that the statement from the Karadzic case is marked as non-associated exhibit. [In English] And we just made a supplementary statement for this witness so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was some confusion about the reference in paragraph 12 of the motion referring to two associated exhibits, where in Annex C I think we did not find an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I would call on the screen 1D2109.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the statement from the Karadzic case. This is the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember giving this statement to the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes. And I testified before this court.

utterances.text: Would you change anything to this statement or would you stand by what you said to Mr. Karadzic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at 1D1629.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see on the left the signature? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, in this statement, 1D1629, we need page 2. Paragraph 2. You told me last night when we had a chance to talk that the indication until when you were an engineer in Energoinvest in charge of long-distance power transmission lines is wrong.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2110 receives number D502. And document 1D2111 receives number D503, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would read summary of the statement of this witness, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war, Veljko Lubura, was engaged in compulsory work service at the Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska. He kept a post of a chief engineer for the distribution of electric energy. Upon reorganisation of the Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska in August 1992, he was appointed director of the Elektroprenos plant in Ilidza. That means electro transmission. In 1992 and later on, Serb company led by Mr. Lubura, tried to repair the Reljevo-Vogosca and Vogosca-Velesici and Vogosca-Sokolac transmission lines but mainly failed to do so because of the combat operations and obstruction by the Muslim side; in particular, the Muslim side obstructing the supply of the Vogosca substation where the Pretis and TAS factories were situated. Those factories were in Serbian hands. Due to these obstructions, the Velesici substation did not receive electric power to transmit it further across the part of the city under Muslim control. In late 1992, the Serbs managed to put in operation the Vogosca-Rogatica-Sokolac transmission line that the Muslim army had damaged in Gornja Lijeska. This created the conditions for the hydropower to start operating with technological minimum. In late 1992, the Serbs tried to distribute electric power to 15 Muslim settlement of Hrasnica. Given that Hrasnica-Blazuj transmission line and cables were cut, they were not able to do this without major repair work, and these were all along the lines of disengagement between the Serbian and Muslim armies. Blazuj substation was shelled by Juka Prazina units, and for this reason the whole area of north western Sarajevo, both Serbian and Muslim parts, remained without electric power supply until the end of January 1993. Blazuj substation was shelled -- sorry. Strike that. The lack of electric power supply in the core city under the Muslim control was due to the failures in the transmission line which usually occurred along the line of disengagement. When such a thing happened, they would negotiate at the airport to carry out joint repair work in the presence of UNPROFOR. On one occasion, while attempting to repair a transmission line, they came under the fire originating from Ugarsko [phoen] which was under Muslim control. With the liberation of Trnovo in July 1993, Serb side managed to repair the Buk Bijela-Lukavica transmission line and thus bring in quality energy power from Montenegro to the Lukavica substation. The company of Mr. Lubura was prepared to transmit further part of the energy to substations in Dobrinja, Otoka, and Skenderija on the Muslim side under the condition that the transmission lines connecting these substations were repaired. However, the Muslim side showed no interest in this proposal. Veljko Lubura responsibly claims that nobody, both from the municipal or republican level, civilian or military authorities, ever ordered him, orally or in writing, to cut off electric power supply to any part of Sarajevo, and he would not done this even if given such instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed. It seems that you have forgotten a bit about the 35 lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm a few lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were shorter last time. Let's leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I really tried with this one. I had four pages so it was not easy to cut down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would propose a few more questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, but not until after I have given an opportunity to Judge Moloto to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, just for my own edification, what do we mean by line of disengagement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it's a line of engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Engagement, yeah. Probably it has to become a line of disengagement if they want to repair something. But ... I would like that have 1D2110. That -- I -- it has a new number. I didn't jot it down probably.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number is D502, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So please put D502 into the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lubura, do you see the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see various numbers here. I'll ask you one by one to proceed faster. We see Sarajevo 7; that's Buca Potok. In whose hands was this transformer station?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: In Muslim hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo 2, Velesici?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: In Muslim hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo 5, Kosevo?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo 13, Skenderija?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: In Muslim hands, 13, 14, 15, and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about 18, Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Also in Muslim hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'll ask you what was in Serb hands. Do you see Reljevo?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Sarajevo 10, Reljevo, was in Serbian hands. It's one of the most powerful one; 400 kilowatts. One of the most powerful in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then Sarajevo 1, Blazuj, next to Ilidza, also in Serb hands. And Sarajevo 20, Lukavica, also in Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo 4, Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: That was also in Serb hands. That was within the compound of the PAS and Pretis -- sorry, TAS and Pretis. It was very close to the separation line. Muslim trenches were very close by. At a distance of up to 500 metres were the Muslim trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the Muslim territory of the city of Sarajevo electricity had to be transmitted through Serb territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the Serbs had stopped the flow of electricity to the Muslims, would they have electricity themselves?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: No, they wouldn't. This entire north-west part of Sarajevo, municipalities Hadzici, Ilidza, Rajlovac, parts of Vogosca and parts of Ilijas, Serbs would not have power either because the transformer station Reljevo was fed by a 110-kilowatt long-distance transmission line from Kiseljak and the connection was either by aerial from Kraka, Mount Jablanica -- Kakanj, sorry, and the hydropower station Jablanica which were under Muslim control. Therefore, if anyone had cut off the power transmission towards the Muslim part of Sarajevo, of course, the Muslims would have cut off power to them immediately. So, in that north-west part of the Sarajevo city, over 100.000 Serbs would be left without electricity and so would the Muslims in the central part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which line of supply was in operation during the war? To the city I mean.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: After the outbreak of the conflict in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, most of the energy assets were immediately damaged to a great extent, and the only two transmission lines that were in operation that we had managed to repair was the supply from Kiseljak to Reljevo, 110-kilowatts, that was the transformer station Sarajevo 10, and from Sarajevo 10 to Buca Potok up to the transformer station Sarajevo 7, that was operating. All the others had suffered major damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about nowadays, are all the lines in operation? What is going on with the Lukavica-Skenderija line?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes. Nowadays all of the lines which had been damaged were repaired in 2003 by virtue of the Power 3 project. The entire semi-circle of -- called Nikola Tesla has been repaired including all 110-kilowatts networks in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Both the federal and the Serbian and the Herzegovina electric boards fixed their respective networks. When it comes to the city of Sarajevo, all the lines are up save for line 20 at Lukavica and the Skenderija 1. That transmission line has not been repaired to date for reasons unbeknownst to me because I no longer work for Elektroprivreda. I have retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are done with this map, and I'd like to see 1D2111 next.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is document D503 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the general area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We can see almost all of it. Concerning this map, can you tell us what happens when the system is left without any transmission lines?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: On this map, we see all 400- and 220- and 110-kilovolt transmission lines in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as connections to the neighbouring republics of Croatia, Montenegro. As regards Serbia, there was no transmission line of 110, 220, and 400 kilovolts. I think this map indicates the situation as of the late 1990s and it was published by the electrical board of the former SFRY. Well, you see, on this map we can see that the entire of Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of the 400 kilovolt semi-ring or semi-circle and the electrical system worked in stable conditions. Most of the large transformer stations received power from different sources, from several sources; for example, Reljevo, which is Sarajevo 10, it received power from several sources like Tuzla, Mostar, and Kakanj. So large transformer stations had multiple sources. If there was a breakdown along one of the high voltage lines, it created instability in the entire electrical supply system. The problem we had during the war was that the system that was in place was very unstable. Most transformer stations had single sources and energy sources also had only one line carrying electricity further afield. It means that no matter where there was a breakdown in the network, it affected the entire network and the entire system could cave in causing electricity to be cut off in wide, very wide area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if I look at this map and especially the "legenda," I see "crvena linija," "zelena linija," and another, "crna linija," but we have no translation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have the legend on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the top, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness. It's maybe the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if it means red line --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it doesn't help that much to say that a red line is a red line is not very helpful in understanding. I take it that it refers to the kilovolt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Red line refers to 400 kilovolts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. I see that. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Zelena linija" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- a green line, 220 kilovolts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had zoomed in too much. But therefore the red lines are the 400 kilovolts, the green lines are the 220, and then the last one was the?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Crna linija," it's black line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The black line, that's 110 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- kilovolt. Thank you. I don't think, unless the Prosecution insists with a translation, that we leave it with this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to have 1D2112 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can read and speak English, Mr. Lubura, can't you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before us is a document signed by -- well, the name at the bottom is that of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. It was sent to General Morillon. It is stated that one day previously an agreement had been reached and Mrs. Plavsic is now forwarding a list of people making up the teams to carry out repairs in the electrical and water networks, water supply networks. In the electricians team we see at number 1, Engineer Veljko Lubura, head of the team. Is that you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes. As for the others, Spasoje Marinkovic was my assistant. Dragan Despotovic was a liaison officer with UNPROFOR, tasked with electricity, water, and gas repairs. However, he was a workmate of mine and we suggested that he be part of the team. People under numbers 4, 5, 6, and 7 were excellent professionals, excellent electricians we used to fix the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We seek to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I don't hear from the party after they had reasonable time to jump up, then I take it that there are no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2112 receives number D504, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. And, Mr. Jeremy, sometimes through eye contact, I try to confirm that you had sufficient time but, nevertheless, did not jump up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you co-operate with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The teams which carried out repairs, were they of single ethnicity or were the people of different ethnicities there? What was the makeup of those teams?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Repairing -- as regards the repair of electrical supply in Serb territory, the teams were Serbian. But in the areas where there were separation lines where there were most damages done by combat, we had joint teams, meaning a Muslim and a Serb team. We would meet with UNPROFOR at a specified location. We knew, more or less, where in the transmission network there was damage, and joint teams went to fix it together. This is high voltage with very tall towers, and usually two Serbs and two Muslims would climb those towers. So the soldiers on either side of the line couldn't tell who was on what tower, and they were usually in civilian clothes or in plain blue work clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the transmission system like during the war? What was the basic difference as compared to the pre-war period?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: The main difference compared to the pre-war period was that during the war the electrical system worked in an instable environment. No matter what caused a breakdown and no matter where in the network it happened, whether it was close to the source or along the transmission lines or in the distribution network, it affected the entire network which would then fall apart. Protection mechanisms would be triggered and the system had to be shut down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What could cause this interruption in the supply of electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Such interruptions were called by the so-called systematic mistakes because the system was inherently unstable. Other causes of breakdowns were, for example, when something malfunctioned in a transformer station itself. Unless you had spare parts, it took a long time. If you did have spare part, it would have been dealt with in one or two days. As for any other problems caused by placing too much burden on the system, it was dealt with by dispatchers on either sides. That could be dealt with in a single day. The third problem for the most part was the physical damage of otherwise operational transmission lines. It usually happened along combat lines and separation lines. For example, let's take Sarajevo 10 or Sarajevo 7 or Reljevo-Buca Potok, that transmission line went across Sokolje hill where there were Muslim forces. The Serb forces were perhaps 5- to 600 metres further down the hill at Mijevica [phoen] Kosa. I am quite familiar with that terrain. So there was less than 500 metres between the two sides, and when there was combat, for example, conductors would be damaged and cables would fall on the ground, short-circuiting the transformer station, the Reljevo transformer station would be shut off immediately and we knew where the breakdown was. In that case we relied on the liaison officer to contact UNPROFOR immediately. UNPROFOR then talked to the military commands on both sides, asking that there was a lull or a truce, so that we could reach the territory where the damage was in no man's land to carry out repairs. It often happened on this particular transmission line. Repairing such breakdowns usually took between four and six days. Situation was even more serious if the Kiseljak-Reljevo transmission line was damaged, meaning that it connected Sarajevo with the source. It would usually happen at Kokoska hill where all the three sides were, so the Serb, the Muslim, and the Croat side had to agree that all three sides give permission for our team to carry out repairs safely. So UNPROFOR needed two or three days to tour all the commands until they received confirmation. Once they did, they would ask us to go into the field to fix it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the situation like in terms of spare parts?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: At first, it was quite all right. But as the war went on, there was -- there were no more spare parts. We particularly had problems with oil for transformer stations because it was difficult to get by, and all -- and the Serbs and Muslims stole such oil because they could use it as fuel for vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many mechanics did you have at your disposal? In other words, people who could carry out repairs?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: In my plant, there were three services. The first and most important service was that of transmission lines repairs. I had a group of four electric technicians and one foreman. As for maintenance, my team was exceptional, with highly trained and highly professional electricians. But in order to maintain the entire network of over 200 kilometres of transmission lines, I would have needed five groups. However, with some super-human effort, we did manage to deal with most of the disruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document 1D3239, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what are we doing with the previous one, the one that was on our screen? The Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Didn't I offer that for admission? If I haven't yet, I would like to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was D504; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I missed that. There's, however, it appears to be in English only in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. That's, I think, sufficient enough. It's UNPROFOR document. We do not translate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we can read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for -- of course, for the public character of the trial, one may wonder whether it not be preferable to have all the evidence available in the two languages. But let's -- let's consider that. It's not such a vital document, but I just noticed that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lubura, we are looking at an UNPROFOR document dated the 15th of June, 1995. I'm going to read the first paragraph, which states: [In English] "At the very last minute, the Bosnian side this afternoon rejected a proposal to restore utilities to Sarajevo. The Serbian side had agreed to the necessary technical agreements [sic] arranged by Mr. John Fawcett from the office of the special co-ordinator for Sarajevo. But the Bosnian side insisted on UNPROFOR control of Bacevo (Sarajevo's main water-pumping station which is on Serb-controlled territory) as well as several gas supply points." [Interpretation] Let me ask you this: In your work, did you ever find the Muslim side to obstruct agreements or prevent repair work. Do you know of any such cases?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I do. I was personally there with a repair team when we tried to repair the transmission line Sarajevo 10 Vogosca. And if we had managed to fix the transmission line, then we could transmit electricity from Sarajevo 10 Reljevo to the Vogosca transformer station. And then after repairing the Vogosca-Velesici line, then we could use a part of that energy and transmit it to the Velesici transformer station which was under Muslim control. I don't recall the date precisely, but I was there personally at Zuc hill. We were assisted by the Spanish battalion. We were fired on. The repair team was a mixed team of Serbs and Muslims, but we were fired at from village of Ugarsko [phoen] which was under Muslim control, and this transmission line was never repaired nor could the teams ever get to it. I know for sure that the Muslim side did not want the Vogosca transformer station to receive electricity because that is where the TAS and Pretis factories were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked not to get so close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you not to come too close to the microphone. The interpreters would prefer you to keep a certain small distance to the microphone. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We would like to tender this document as MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D3239 receives number D505, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Also in view of the lack of a B/C/S translation, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I noted this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Yes, it's MFI'd, under the number given by Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any technical reasons why the Muslim side could not have more electric power?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes. I will explain that. The Buca Potok or Sarajevo 10 to Reljevo line, we were unable to pass on -- through more electricity, 20 plus 3, as we had agreed with the Muslim side, plus -- 20 plus 3 megawatts for the Serbian side. But the Buca Potok capacity was 23.5 mva, so we could not transfer more electricity to Buca Potok. We could have done it had the transmission line Reljevo Vogosca been repaired and the Vogosca-Velasevic line. When Trnovo was liberated afterwards and when we got electricity in Lukavica, had the transmission lines leading towards Dobrinja, Potokci [phoen], and Skenderija been repaired -- well, the Skenderija transmission line was heavily damaged, but these other two that went via Mojmilo through Potoka [phoen] and Mojmilo could have been repaired. Of course, as electricity was coming from Montenegro, it would have to have been paid for, of course. I was prepared to do that as the director, and I even suggested at a meeting with UNPROFOR that after getting the Lukavica transformer station up and going, to repair the transmission lines two times 110 Lukavica Dobrinja and Lukavica Otoka, this is one and the same transmissions line which forks off to different transformer stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question here, Mr. Lukic. You said you had agreed 20 plus 3 megawatts for the Muslim side, and 20 plus 3 megawatts for the Serbian side, but you couldn't deliver that because of the capacity of the line. Now, how did you then -- you were short of, if I understand you well, close to 23 megawatts which you couldn't deliver. How did you divide that between the -- if I could say so, the customers? Did you cut both parties down the same way, or did you -- or did you deliver a higher percentage to the Muslims, or a higher percentage to the Serbs? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain that. It is a technical matter, so I do know it. I will try to be as simple as possible so that everyone can understand. The agreement between Serbs and Muslims at the Sarajevo airport was to provide 20 plus 3 megawatts from the Reljevo transformer station should go to Buca Potok. We could not send more power through Buca Potok because the capacity of the transformer was 20.5. Had the transformer station had a greater capacity at Buca Potok, we could have provided more electricity to Buca Potok. It was 20.3. So the agreement was 20 megawatts to go to Sarajevo under Muslim control under the condition that these three megawatts should be passed on to Grbavica which was under Serb control. And 20 plus 3 megawatts from the Sarajevo 10 Reljevo transformer station was sent to the Blazuj transformer station from where we supplied the Serb areas with 20 megawatts, this was Hadzici, Ilijas, Rajlovac, and Ilidza, and the 3 megawatts we were obliged to provide through the distribution lines to the pump systems at the Konjac and Bacevo sources so that the water supply could be kept operational, both for the Serb and Muslim parts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I therefore do understand that where the capacity was insufficient that both parties were limited in the electricity they would receive and that some parts were reserved for special destinations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. Well, I'm looking at the clock. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to finish as soon as possible. Five to seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five to seven minutes. I leave it to you whether you want to finish now the five, seven minutes, and take the break slightly later. Perhaps also depends on what Mr. Mladic's preference is, and your preference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to finish, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll go on for another five to seven minutes and the Prosecution will then start its cross-examination after the break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lubura, did you do everything that you could to provide regular electricity, both to the Serb and the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Not just I myself but all the Elektroprenos employees which I headed. We all give our utmost for the Serb and Muslim side to have regular electricity supplies because then we would sleep with a clear conscience. We simply tried to provide both sides with sufficient quantities of electricity, at least for the basic necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who would the Serbian side have to ask in order to cut electricity off to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: As for cutting off the electricity supply, they would have had to ask me, because I was the director of that particular plant. So they would have to ask me to turn the electricity off, to shut it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And were you ever asked to do that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: No, never. Neither orally or in writing. As the plant director, I state this with full responsibility. I said the same thing in the case against President Karadzic. Nobody ever asked that, particularly not from the highest level, but this was not the case at lower levels of authority, municipality presidents, Executive Board presidents, brigade commander, no. My unit covered 15 municipalities if we're talking about civilian authorities. As for the military authorities, I think that my plant covered a territory of some three corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija one, partly the Drina Corps, and a part -- another corps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If everybody was in a position to issue orders to me, I don't know what I would have done. My person who ordered -- who gave me orders was the director of the electrical production industry of Elektroprivreda, also Mr. Skulic who was his deputy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please be asked to repeat this last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were the only ones who could issue such an order to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said, and I read what is on the transcript. The person who gave me orders was the director of the electrical production industry of Elektroprivreda, also Mr. Skulic, who was his department -- That is where it becomes unclear. Could you re -- could you again give your answer, starting with that the director of the electrical protection industry of Elektroprivreda gave you orders and then what you said after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people that I answered to and who were issuing orders to me were the general director of Elektroprivreda, of the Republika Srpska, Dr. Milorad Skoko. The technical director of Elektroprivreda, Drago Skulic, and the main director of Elektroprenos, Engineer Dragoljub Davidovic. Only those three people could issue an order to me as to what to do and how to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then also seek clarification of one of your previous answers. I'll read to you what is on the transcript in English. You were asked whether you were ever asked to cut off -- to turn off the electricity, and you said: "No, never. Neither orally or in writing. As the plant director, I state this with full responsibility." And then you said: [As read] "I said the same thing in the Karadzic case. Nobody ever asked that, particularly not from the highest level, but this was not the case at lower levels of authority, municipality presidents, Executive Boards presidents, brigade commander, no." Now, what did you mean when you said this was not the case at lower levels. Does that mean that the lower levels had asked you to turn off the electricity, or that it was done at lower levels without your knowledge? Could you please explain what you meant by those words, that it was not the case at lower levels of authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the lower level of authority, they were not the ones who could issue orders to me. They could never instruct me what to do, and I would not listen to those instructions either about cutting electricity off. I'm only talking about high voltage cuts. So they could not have and they did not issue such instructions to me. As the plant director, I never received any oral or written orders from the highest to the lowest level of authority to cut off electricity to the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you said the higher authorities could have asked for it but they didn't, and the lower authorities could not ask for it and they never did either. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, one additional question. You said, I was exclusively talking about the high voltage cuts. Do you know anything of cuts at the lower voltage lines or relay stations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that I had so much work at Elektroprenos. Besides being the director of the Ilidza plant, I'm an electrical engineer, so I participated in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether you know anything of cuts at a lower voltage level, why you would know or not know that is a different question. But do you know anything of cuts, electricity cuts at a lower voltage lines? Did it happen? Did it never happen? Don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it could have happened, but you do not know about it. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, one final clarification. You said, Witness, that your plant covered a territory of some three corps: The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and partly the Drina Corps. And what was the third?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm afraid that we stole three or four minutes from your time already. If you have -- if you want to take them back, then have you an opportunity now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Orie asked you about cuts on lower voltage lines. How does that work? Could that be done manually? Because I don't know. In theory, could somebody cut such a low voltage line or could it be only a result of damage? Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Lower voltage lines, that's -- that means 10 kv or lower. I don't know if we had any such around Sarajevo. I don't think so. I believe the Muslim side received power supply only through the 110 kv transmission line. It didn't work by sending lower voltage from the Serb territory to the Muslim territory, no. Such things didn't happen, as far as the Sarajevo area is concerned. Because lower voltage lines could either be cut manually or switched off at transformer stations, or simply cut the line. That's concerning Sarajevo. But as for the Muslim part of Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the energy they received was through the 110 transmission line, long-distance transmission line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. In the previous answer, I noticed that the answer started by: "I don't know if we had any such around Sarajevo. I don't think so. I believe the Muslim side received," et cetera. It is not knowing. It is believing. It's if we have concrete information, we'd like to hear it. But to hear a long story on the basis of what the witness says what he believes or -- and I take it that will be possible to provide such information. Nevertheless, the witness explained already quite a bit about what could be done in a situation of which we do not know whether it existed or not. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I understand differently what you just said. Did you mean you don't know or you are not aware that such a method of transmission existed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Between the Muslim and Serb part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: The only supply was through the 110 kv. Apart from the part of Grbavica which was supplied from the Muslim side through the 10 kv network. That's what we sent through the lower voltage line to Buca Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's try to finish within a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 10788 is the document we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here a decision which is not directly related to electrical energy but to water. We see the war committee of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza adopted a decision on the 4th of August, 1992, to suspend water supply to Ilidza in the city of Sarajevo from Bacevo until further notice and the reasons are stated below. That means constant shelling and damage to the water supply lines and also that the well had been bombed. My question is: The water supply network in Sarajevo and its feed, did they depend on electricity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo, Mr. Lukic, and I know these things well. As for the main supply of the city of Sarajevo, it came from the sources of Bacevo and Konaci. However, the city of Sarajevo had two other major sources: Tilova and Bistrica, just below Mount Jahorina which went down to the old town where we had a small hydropower plant and the Serb side never cut off water from there. However, these two major sources, Bacevo and Konaci, the water comes from wells. Each well has its own pump and its own transformer station, 10/.4 kilovolts, and all these pumps pump out the water from the soil, send it to main reservoirs, and from these reservoirs in Bacevo and Konaci the water goes to the water supply at Mojmilo hill. According to the Muslim-Serb deal from the transformer station of Blazuj in Sarajevo 1, we provided up to 10 megawatts of electricity for the pumps, the water-pumps, at Bacevo and Konaci, and my dispatchers observed this deal. They sent the electricity. But what happened over there when there was shelling or when the pump broke down or when the transformer station broke down, that was out of my power.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One final question. Did you know if the Muslim forces shelled Bacevo?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there was frequent shelling. The hospital was shelled. Even my transformer station was shelled by Jukaprazina. It was the longest period for Sarajevo without electricity because Jukaprazina's units shelled the transformer station Sarajevo 1 on the 12th of December and they damaged all my transformers, the oil leaked out. I was not unable [as interpreted] to repair more than one. And up to the 29th of January, 1993, neither the Muslim nor the Serb side had electricity, and thereby they didn't even have water because the units of Jukaprazina had shelled the transformer station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So simple answer is, yes, it happened. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was my last question. I just wanted to ask for this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10788 receives number D506, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D506 is admitted. We take a break. Witness, you'll be escorted out of the courtroom, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start the cross-examination, I will deliver a statement. The text which is distributed to the booths is, in the beginning and at the end, slightly differs from the statement I will make. The Chamber will now deliver a statement in response to the Prosecution's proposal to tender transcript of prior cross-examination of witnesses as part of its cross-examination in this case. The statement does also gives the reasons why the Chamber decided to deny the application for tendering prior testimony and associated exhibits for Witness Lubura. On the 28th of April of this year, and the 2nd, the 12th, and the 19th of May, the Prosecution proposed that it be allowed to tender portions of a witness's previous cross-examination in the Karadzic case in order to save court time. The Prosecution submits that such prior testimony should be admitted under Rule 92 bis or, in the alternative, Rule 89(C) and (F) of the Rules. The Prosecution cited an Appeals Chamber decision in the Aleksovski case of the 16th of February 1999 in support of its proposal. All this can be found in Prosecution filings of the 28th of April, the 2nd of May, and at transcript pages 21020 up to and including 21022 and 21037 up to and including 21044. The Defence responded on the 19th and the 26th of May of this year, objecting to the proposal. The Defence submits that the practice employed during the Prosecution's case should be followed; namely, that prior cross-examination is put to the witness and that confirmation of such testimony is then sought. The Defence submits that changing this practice now would violate the principle of equality of arms between the parties. The Defence also submits that Mr. Karadzic is self-respected and, as such, without the benefit of trained counsel, may not have raised necessary objections to certain questions of the Prosecution. Lastly, the Defence points to a decision of the Karadzic Trial Chamber which states that the cross-examining party should pose any questions to the witness directly, instead of tendering prior testimony through Rule 92 ter. At the outset, the Chamber notes that pending its decision on the matter, the Prosecution to date has adopted the approach of confronting witnesses with their previous cross-examination and seeking confirmation or clarification. While this approach may result in slightly longer cross-examinations, in the view of the Chamber it increases the clarity of the presentation of evidence by directly confronting the witness, thus also making it easier for the Chamber to pose additional questions and determine a witness's credibility. Under these circumstances, it is the Chamber's strong preference that the Prosecution continue this practice. For Witness Lubura, the Prosecution made an application to tender prior testimony and associated exhibits. Considering the Chamber's strong preference for receiving the Prosecution's cross-examination orally, the Chamber denies this application. Finally, the Prosecution submits that court time may be saved by tendering maps marked by the witness in a prior case together with the examination of that map. The Chamber is not convinced that such tendering would enhance the clarity of the evidence of a witness. In addition, re-marking of a map would not be the only other way to get this evidence before the Chamber. For example, the Prosecution could tender the previously marked map and seek confirmation from the witness in relation to the markings. This concludes the Chamber's statement on this matter. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, the -- the confusion about how to spell the name of the witness would have been avoided if you would, as is usually done, would have put as the first question to the witness to tell us his name and his date of birth. That would have avoided any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lubura.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In your direct examination you discussed a couple of maps, in particular P503. This is a map of the electricity grid in Bosnia. I'd like to start by showing you another map, also the electricity grid in Bosnia, which I hope is a little more legible than P503. Excuse me, D503.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 30735. And, Your Honours, I have colour copies of this map in A3, which I'll -- I would ask the Court Officer to provide to you in case it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If they exist already then there's no reason not to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, as this is being brought to our screen, I can tell you that it's a map of the BiH power system taken from the web site of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe, the OSCE, and it's a map that's dated 13th of September 2010. Now this is a map that was presented to you during your cross-examination in the Karadzic case. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: It's the same map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. In your --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Are you ready for me to proceed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In your testimony in that case, you confirmed that with the exception of the Bosanski Petrovac-Kljuic transmission line, this map reflects the same electrical grid in Bosnia that was in place between 1992 and 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: There are minor differences. I'll explain. Here you have a long distance transmission line of 400 kv, thermal power station Ugljevik, Sremska Mitrovica, that was made in 2003 through the Power 3 European Union -- European bank loan. Also, you have here a long transmission line of 220 kv, Visegrad, going to Uzicka Pozega. That transmission line did not exist before the war. And here you have a 110 kv long transmission line Visegrad-Rudo-Modric. There used to be a transmission line up to Rudo of 110, but during the war we made a long transmission line 110 of about 8.5 kilometres in order to be able to start the hydropower plant Visegrad. So this map is identical to the one shown from -- shown in 1990 by YUTEL.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. On this map we see from Visegrad the green 220 kilovolt line going east into Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, that was made in 1998, I think. That means after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we also see a green 220 kilovolt line going just below Foca into Montenegro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes. I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, I just would like to confirm that it is in fact the 220 kilovolt line going into Serbia. I don't need a further explanation at this stage.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, this is 220 kv long transmission line made before the war between the hydropower plant Piva. It reaches Foca, that is Buk Bijele, where a hydropower plant was to be built. And then it is connected to a 400 kv long transmission line going towards Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, please carefully listen to the questions, and I assume that could you tell us for hours further explanations on lines and their history. But, first, answer the question and limit it to that. Mr. Jeremy, page 34, line 12. That is 220 kilovolt, I take it. And you said going into Montenegro, whereas later you said going into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I misspoke. I meant to say Montenegro the second time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second time you intended to say Montenegro as well. Please proceed. And that's the line below -- south of Foca, whereas, the newer line near Visegrad was the one which now goes into Serbia. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I tender that map as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the witness been provided with a hard copy? It's the same as what he sees on his screen. He has commented on it. But I don't know whether you want to further use it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I don't intend to further use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we leave it as it is. The witness has given his comments. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30735 receives number P6550, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6550 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, today you have confirmed that electricity had to pass through Serb-held territory in order to reach Bosnian-held territory in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you confirmed in your sworn testimony in the Karadzic case that it was possible for the Bosnian Serbs to prevent the delivery of electricity to Bosnian Muslim-held territory in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: They were able to get it, yes -- they were able to prevent it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to now discuss your responsibilities as director of the Elektroprenos plant in Ilidza. Now, you commenced this role in August 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you ended your duties as director there in mid-May 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were responsible for the administration and the maintenance of substations and transmission lines in Serb-controlled territory in the Sarajevo area; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Not only Sarajevo, but also further afield. The plant that I managed covered a much larger territory. There were 15, 110, and 400 kv transformer stations. And it was a much larger region. As the chief engineer, I worked under the instructions of the general director, and in the Posavina valley through the corridor we started the hydropower plant Ugljevik to Zvornik. So my main activity together with the director was the plant in Ilidza that covered 15 Serb municipalities, plus the extra orders of the general manager to me as an electrical engineer to restore -- in fact, establish the electrical grid to supply Krajina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the Doboj region and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple answer to the question therefore is: Yes, although my area of responsibility was wider than just Sarajevo. That would have been the short answer without all the details. Mr. Jeremy, it's also for you to -- unless you were specifically focusing on these details which the witness then gave spontaneously. But I doubt [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: My question had a narrow focus, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Try to keep in control. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, when repairs were required within the Sarajevo area within the territory in which you operated, it was your company that sent the technicians to carry out that work. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And sometimes those repairs would be carried alongside UNPROFOR, together with technicians from the Bosnian Muslim side; yes?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: That's right. When there were breakdowns on supply lines, joint teams would go out to deal with it with the presence of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So your role was to use your technical knowledge to carry out necessary repairs; yes?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in order for those repairs to be carried out on the confrontation line, approval of access for technical teams was required by the Bosnian Serb army and the ABiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that approval from the warring parties was obtained not by you but by UNPROFOR; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: UNPROFOR would contact the warring parties; the Serb and the Muslim side. Once they have obtained approval, a guarantee that there would be no combat in the areas of repairs, we would send joint teams to carry out those repairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 8 of your new statement for the Mladic case -- in fact, let's provide you with a hard copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If the usher could please assist. And also provide a copy of the statement from the Karadzic, please, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, before we continue, is it clear to you which of the copies is your statement in the Karadzic case and which was the newly produced statement for this case? Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the supplemental part. The basic, original statement is the one I provided in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see D501. That's the statement, the new statement, for this case. The supplemental statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, I'd like you to take a look at paragraph 8 of your new statement. There, you refer to failures to electricity transmission systems and you state: "Failures were operational or mechanical and were mostly caused by war operations." Mr. Lubura, this leaves open the possibility for damaged lines to stay damaged for long periods of time due to, for example, denial of access to repairs, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: When there were mechanical repairs needed due to war operations, such repairs took longer to be fixed, as I stated in my first statement. Once we have established there was a breakdown, which would usually come -- appear between the separation lines, we would turn to the liaison officer and the service for co-operation with UNPROFOR at Lukavica in the SRK. We would then notify UNPROFOR and UNPROFOR would in turn ask approval by both sides which, once obtained, would enable a joint team to go in the field and fix it. It could take anywhere between five and eight days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I can't recall off the cuff how many such repairs were required because it was 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, I'm going to stop you here because you're repeating yourself. The question was whether this also still leaves open the possibility that, because access was denied, that, for that reason, the transmission system was not functioning for a longer period of time. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I don't know how the warring parties reacted to UNPROFOR's requests for us to go out in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did it happen that no access was given, and for -- that for that reason the transmission system on that part was not functioning for a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that and I can't confirm it. Such malfunctions were usually dealt with between five and eight days at the most, but I don't know what was the main cause of it. I don't know whether one of the sides prevented such repairs. I really can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, is it your evidence that you were not aware that the Bosnian Serb side denied access to repair lines, to lines that required -- that needed to be repaired. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: No. Yes, I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document, 65 ter 30736. And while it's being brought up on the screen, Mr. Lubura, I can tell you it's a report for July 1993 from the UNPROFOR sector engineer for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And Mr. Lubura we see that this document is signed by Lieutenant-Colonel M. Maufrais, sector engineer. Now, in paragraph 9 of your supplemental statement, D501, you refer to a French UNPROFOR battalion that assisted in resolving technical issues relating to power supply. And you refer to a Major Mofrez, M-o-f-r-e-z. Is this the same person as this Colonel Maufrais we see here?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I know Mr. Maufrais excellently. He was a major at first and later probably became a lieutenant-colonel. We co-operated excellently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: At first he was a major and then later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I think by your answer, unless there's any reason to belive there were two Lieutenant-Colonels Maufrais moving around that it is the same. Please proceed. You said you worked together with him perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 1 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I -- I know that you understand English, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But the B/C/S translation has just been uploaded and it is available. Perhaps we can look at them side by side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, we see the subheading: "Utility Situation." It states: "Getting worse and worse since the beginning of the war, the utilities situation in July for Sarajevo area has been the most critical. Sarajevo was never so strongly besieged." Two paragraphs down we see it says: "It is to notice that the Serbian controlled area was fully fed with water and almost fully fed with electricity." I would also like do draw your attention to paragraph 11 at the bottom of the page, subheading: "Electricity." It states: [As read] "Electricity is and will remain the key of all the utilities problems inside the sector. All the repairs are connected with. Serbs denied any access to the repair location on the line which is supplying the town (Reljevo Vogosca)."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy you read "repairs." It reads "all the others are connected," the others apparently referring to other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, given your close relationship, your working relationship with the author of this document, is this something that you were aware of at the time, this denial of access to the repair locations that Colonel Maufrais is talking about here in this report?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Well, if you look at paragraph 11, "Electricity," one can read that the Serbs denied access to a number of locations such as Reljevo and Vogosca. The transmission line between Reljevo and Vogosca could supply Vogosca and then further afield to Velesici. However, the main power of electricity for the Muslim part of Sarajevo went through the transmission line Reljevo and Buca Potok; in other words, the city of Sarajevo did have electricity at the time through Reljevo-Buca Potok transmission line. Reljevo-Vogosca line is where there was fierce combat at Zuc, and of course we tried to fix it. I don't know whether it was precisely in the month Mr. Maufrais drafted this report, but the city of Sarajevo did receive electricity through the Reljevo-Buca Potok transaction line. This transmission line Mr. Maufrais is referring to between Reljevo and Vogosca had to do with supplying the Vogosca transformer station, and via Vogosca that electricity could have been carried onto Velesici, and then the city of Sarajevo would have more electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question was not answered, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, were you aware in July 1993 that the Serbs were denying access to the repair location on the line which is supplying the town Reljevo-Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I have explained to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that the city of Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- received electricity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- from a different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question is not whether Sarajevo received electricity. The question is whether you were aware that the Serbs denied access for repairs. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it has to do with a different transmission line between Reljevo and Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there was combat there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware that the Serbs denied access on the line indicated for repairs? That's the simple question. If you were aware, tell us; if you were not aware, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't aware. I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I tendered that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30736 receives number P6551, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, you don't know that the Serb side made access for repair teams in Sarajevo conditional on political concessions by the Bosnian Muslim side, do you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you know -- you also don't know whether the Serb side made access for repair teams in Sarajevo conditional on military concessions by the Bosnian Muslim side, do you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, during the war the Sokolac-Vogosca line was not repaired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: The Sokolac-Vogosca transmission line was not repaired near Vogosca in the area of Poljine village because the Muslim side never allowed us to do so. On the contrary, when we set out to repair that part of the transmission line, fire was opened from the Muslim side. The reason why they didn't allow us to fix it was to prevent supply of electricity to the Pretis and TAS companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, as a consequence of this failure to repair the line, the Bosnian Serbs connected a transmission line Poljine-Pale in order to get electricity from Visegrad to Vogosca. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes. And I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this way you were able to get power to the Pretis factory; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes. I installed eight MVAs of transformer power. I used it to feed electricity to Vogosca, parts of Ilijas, and the Pretis and TAS factories. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 of your supplemental statement, which if we could please take a look at D501, there you refer to assistance that were provided with by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and you refer to their assistance with transporting electrical equipment and in particular high power transformers. I'd like to show you a document in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 30747. This is a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps document from Dragomir Milosevic to the VRS Main Staff dated 30 September 1993. Could we take a look at page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, in the third paragraph down, we see that it states: "Given that we need a power supply, it is our preventative interest to get a power supply ring installed in Republika Srpska and thereby obtain sufficient electricity, primarily for military needs but also for other consumers in Grbavica." Mr. Lubura, is this the co-ordination with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that you are referring to in that paragraph in your new statement?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, one of them. I asked that a 40-tonne transformer station be moved from Reljevo to Lukavica in order to provide quality electricity to Miljevici, Kasindol, Grbavica, and Vrace because before the war they received electricity through 35 kv transmission lines from Sarajevo 18. Those were cut off. And when the Serb side took Trnovo, I fixed the 400 kv transmission line from Trnovo, thus bringing in electricity from Montenegro to Lukavica. But there was no distribution voltage that would be necessary to distribute it, so I had to insert the transformer point. There was a typo here, and it doesn't concern kilowatts but kilovolts. And I asked the SRK command to assist with the transport of the transformer point via some forested area to Lukavica. I managed to do so and I managed to feed electricity to the south-eastern of Sarajevsko Polje which was under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, it's in paragraph 14 of your new statement, D501, referring to your co-ordination with the VRS, you then state: "All this in order to provide better supply for both parts of Sarajevo." Now this document shows that you were co-ordinating with the SRK to provide better power supply to the VRS and the Serb-controlled areas of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Well, of course, I wanted to feed electricity to the Serb side first, being Serbian myself. But at meetings at the airport with the Muslim side, I suggested that I should fix the two times 110 transmission line between Lukavica and Otoka and Nedzarici to Dobrinja so that they too would receive some of electricity. They would receive more electricity from Lukavica which came from the source in Montenegro. I believe you have that document, and you can see there that we discussed the fixing of that transmission line so that the Muslim side, too, would receive more electricity from Lukavica. However, it did not materialise throughout the war, or at least while I managed the plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: On the basis of this document, you would agree with me, yes, that it shows that it's concerned with power supply to the VRS for military needs and for consumers in Grbavica; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the document says, Mr. Jeremy, so there's no -- whether the witness agrees or not. The witness has explained to us that at this moment in relation to this document that may be true but that was not his exclusive focus. His focus was broader and was also, and gave examples of that, to provide the Muslim side with electricity as well. So there's no need, I think, to ask the witness to confirm what the document says. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30747 receives number P6552, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we please see the witness's statement from the Karadzic case, D500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Madam Registrar, could you please repeat the number. It's not appearing on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30747 receives number P6552, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lubura, I'd like you to take a look at paragraph 13 of that statement, please. There you say that the Serbs were prepared to transmit energy to the substations in Dobrinja, Otoka, and Skenderija. I think you mentioned this again in your direct examination this morning. You say that the Muslims showed no interest in this proposal; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 30740.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, if we take a look at the first page and it lists -- under list of delegates, we see Bosnian Serb delegation, 7 c, Veljko Lubura. That's you; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 2, please, and halfway down we see the subheading: "Situation of Repairs." In 2.4 we see a reference to: "LCL Ricquet talked about problems between BSA and UNPROFOR. He said that Serbian side obstructs the works by shooting at the teams. Are the works going to be performed or should the teams withdrawn? The repairs on electric power networks are also political problems [sic]. These repairs are being performed on the BH side, but not on the Bosnian Serb side."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we can just go forward, please, to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see 4.3 b, the transmission lines Jablanica-Hadzici-Blazuj-Blazuj Famos-Lukavica, and Lukavica-Otoka-Nedzarici were agreed to be top priority. Mr. Lubura, contrary to what you say in paragraph 13 of your statement about the Muslims showing no interest in the proposal to repair the Lukavica-Otoka transmission line, this document shows that in fact both sides agreed that it would be a top priority; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I remember this meeting well, my memory serves me well. This was my suggestion. I proposed also that the transmission line between Jablanica, Hadzici and Blazuj be repaired. It was heavily damaged. This was my proposal.
