As for why it was never implemented on my part and on behalf of Elektroprenos, which I headed, we were prepared to do this, but we would need to ask the gentlemen on the Muslim side why the repairs were never carried out. During the war this transmission line was never repaired. Perhaps they were afraid. I don't know what they were afraid of. But as far as I'm concerned, I was prepared. I know that at that time they were working on a transmission line through Igman and then they brought the cables down. Perhaps that's why they didn't do it. But I know that they placed a transformer station in the village of Zovik. They went by air on the other side of Igman and then they dropped the cables down on this side that looks on Sarajevo. Electricity had to be paid for, and the electricity that came to Lukavica was coming from Montenegro, so that had to be paid for. I mean, I don't know. This is what I proposed at the meeting. As the director of Prenos, on my side there was no obstruction to fix this. Yes, it was a difficult job, the transmission line was heavily damaged, but it could have been repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30740 receives number P6553, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness, you gave a lot of possible reasons and you said perhaps this or perhaps that's why they didn't do that. In the meeting apparently the -- Mr. Ricquet says, We have problems because the Serbs are shooting when a team intends to repair the line. Now, you come up with a lot of explanations of what possibly may have been the case, but this was reported by someone on the spot. What's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that -- I don't know whether Mr. Ricquet was being fair here or not. I wasn't on the lines each time. I don't know who opened fire. When I was there and when fire was opened, I can confirm this before this Trial Chamber, but I think that it states here in this paper that both sides were shooting. I know that they were shooting when the attempt was made to repair the Vogosca-Velesici transmission line, but I state responsibly that as far as the Sokolac-Vogosca transmission line was concerned, the Serb side never opened fire because it was on their territory. It was the Muslim side that opened fire there because they would not permit electricity to be transmitted to Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not what Mr. Ricquet says, but he apparently has another observation. Please proceed, Mr. -- no, before I encourage you to proceed, Mr. Jeremy, I would rather look at the clock and let's take a break. How far -- could we first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break, and we'll see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where are we in terms of time, Mr. Jeremy and Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would expect to conclude in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then there would be at least some time left for you, Mr. Lukic. If we take another break, it would still be another 25 minutes left. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 30 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom, I must say I appreciate highly that our transcriber may have hidden a mistake I made. I think I said that we'll resume 20 minutes past 12.00, which was obviously a mistake because it would have left us only a break of ten minutes. For all those who appeared early, I apologise, and whenever I can give you ten minutes somewhere for whatever reason - ten minutes' more sunshine, or ten minutes' more something else - please do not hesitate to apply for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, let's stay on the topic of meetings between the Bosnian Serb side, the Bosnian Muslim side, and UNPROFOR. Now, in paragraph 10 of your supplemental statement, D501 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we call it onto our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: While it's coming up, Mr. Lubura, I'll paraphrase that paragraph 10. You refer to -- to the meetings that I've just made reference to. You say the subject of those meetings was to put in order lines that were not operational. You said representatives of the Muslim side "simply never responded to what was agreed at these meetings." In connection with this statement in your witness statement, I would like to refer you to another document, and that's 65 ter 30731. And while that's coming to our screens, Mr. Lubura, I'll tell that you these are minutes from a meeting held at the airport on the 3rd of February 1995. We see of those persons present, at the top of the page a Mr. Jacques Perreaux. Now you refer to a person of the name Pero, P-e-r-o, in paragraph 9 of your statement. This is the same person, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct. Jacques Perreaux. It's French so probably they didn't know how to transcribe it correctly. But yes, Jacques Perreaux, Lieutenant-Colonel Jacques Perreaux.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the BH delegation we see a reference to Dubravka, Nikolic. You refer to him in paragraph 13 of your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, that is Mrs. Dubravka Nikolic. She was the director for development at the Elektroprivreda of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was the Muslim Elektroprivreda, electrical utility company.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'll shortly take you to another page on this document, but out of fairness I'll note that you're not present at this meeting, or at least the minutes indicate that you were not present; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3 in this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, I'd like to focus your attention on the subheading: "Repair Missions in Sarajevo Area." You see "Velesici-Kosevo." "The repair has not been performed yet. The representative of Sector Sarajevo said that BH side had accepted to have a mixed team for the repair and that all necessary authorisations had been obtained, but a local BS commander had not allowed the team to do the repair on 22nd of February, 1995." Mr. Lubura, you would agree, would you not, that contrary to paragraph 10 of your statement, this document states that the Muslim side had responded to what had been agreed at a previous meeting, but in this case the Bosnian Serb side, and in fact a commander of the Bosnian Serb military, had obstructed the repair; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: The Velesici-Kosevo transmission line does not pass through the territory controlled by Bosnian Serbs. So this is not clear to me. The Kosevo-Velesici transmission line is on the Muslim side, 100 per cent. So it's not clear to me how they could have written this and how they could have agreed with it. You can see from the maps that we looked at earlier that the Velesici-Kosevo transmission line passes through practically the centre of town, and I think the Serbian army wasn't even able to shoot at that section of the power transmission line. It's really not clear to me how they could have said something like that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you introduced the document as dating from the 3rd of February. I may -- I assume that you wanted to say 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me just double-check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, the document in this paragraph talks about the 22nd so that couldn't be discussed on the 3rd. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30731 receives number P6554, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, today you've explained that your responsibilities extended beyond the Sarajevo area. Now, it is true, isn't it, that the Bosnian Serbs made power, electrical power, to Sarajevo conditional on power to Serb territory elsewhere; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Probably so. I wasn't at this meeting. However, the meeting which was attended by representatives from Banja Luka I know because I was a member of the Elektroprivreda collegium, the Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska, we had meetings at least twice and we discussed the supply problems of the entire Republika Srpska. I know that the whole of Bosnian Krajina and the Banja Luka region, the Doboj region, did not have enough electricity. Semberija, including Bijeljina, did not have electricity. They just had a part of their electrical supplies coming from Serbia through the Ljesnica-Bijeljina 35 kv route but it was insufficient, and naturally the Serbs were also asking to have electricity for all of their population throughout the whole territory, which is normal. The sources were mostly on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In connection with that answer I'd like to show you a document, 65 ter 3037 [sic]. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, this is a code cable from UNPROFOR Zagreb to UN headquarters. It's entitled: "Briefing Requested by Security Council." It's dated the 27th of October 1994. Now, in paragraph 1 b, we read: [As read] "Electricity (see attachment) repairs have begun on the Sarajevo network following Karadzic's agreements to clear the access of repair teams, provided UNPROFOR subsequently also address the problem of the eastern and northern Bosnian power lines, of particular interest to the Serb civilian populations ..." Were you aware of this agreement by President Karadzic, Mr. Lubura?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rarely object if the document is official document, but I don't think that this witness is good to introduce having in mind his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Jeremy tendered it without saying whether he tendered it as an exhibit related to this witness or whether he wanted to tender it from the bar table because I think that exceptionally if a document is directly linked to the evidence of a witness, although the witness may not have knowledge of that document, and when the document is relevant and may have probative value, that it can be tendered under those circumstances. Would you also object against it be tendered from the bar table?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I will withdraw my objection. I will leave it to Your Honours whether you accept it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second please. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30737 receives number P6555, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. You wanted to say something, Witness. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I were to read the whole document, I would probably have my own comments, but because there isn't enough time -- I mean, I'm sure I would have some comments of mine, and I could clarify some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any factual knowledge, please tell us what it is. If not, we'll proceed. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, today during your direct examination, you've confirmed that you had an agreement with the Bosnian Muslim side that along the Reljevo-Buca Potok transmission line, 20 megawatts of electricity would be provided to Buca Potok, and 3 megawatts would be provided onto Grbavica. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in your Karadzic testimony and again today, you have stated that the only transmission line that was functioning, taking electricity to the centre of Sarajevo was this Reljevo-Buca Potok transmission line; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, at meetings that you attended, you personally stated that power to Buca Potok may be switched off if Grbavica is not given enough power; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In connection with that I'd like to show you a document, 65 ter 30732. And these are minutes of a meeting between representatives of UNPROFOR, ABiH, and the VRS regarding repair of infrastructure in the Sarajevo area dated 10th of February, 1993. Mr. Lubura, we see a -- a reference to names that are mentioned in your new witness statement, P501. We see a reference to Major Maufrais, we see a reference a Durmic, in paragraph 11 of your statement refers to Irfan Durmic. This is the same person; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes. The director of Elektroprenos in Sarajevo, Irfan Durmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I see a reference to Lubura. That's you, correct.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you recall this meeting on the 10th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Well, there were lots of meetings. I don't remember it precisely. Now I'm reading it trying to just remember what the agenda of that meeting was. We had many meetings, so after 20 years I cannot remember each individual one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I understand. And take a moment to familiarise yourself with the document, if you need it. I'd like to ask you a specific question on the document on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And there, the minutes suggest that you made the following comment: "I think that Buca Potok may be switched off if Grbavica does not get enough power." Mr. Lubura, is this -- this is a threat by you, is it not, that power to Buca Potok would be cut off if Serb-held Grbavica does not get enough power; right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Well, I'm not making any threats. This is agreement, you know, between myself and Durmic, meaning 20 megawatts we would give to the inner area of the Muslim part of Sarajevo and the extra 3 megawatts should be passed to Grbavica, where the civilian population, Serbs, were living, but in Grbavica, there were Muslims, Croat, Serbians -- Serbs. So the inner centre of town had to receive a minimum amount of electricity. Grbavica had a large number of citizens. This was part of the city centre held by the Serbs. If we reached some sort of agreement, we had to stick to it. It was not a threat, meaning if we had agreed that we would provide 20 megawatts from Reljevo to the Muslim side plus 3 kilowatts which they would then pass to another part of the centre of town, they had to respect that meeting. We stuck to our part of the bargain to provide 3 megawatts from the Bacevo transformer station to the pumping station area. We did that. As for whether all the pumps were functional or not, this is not my area of professional expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I was not making any threats. I was just asking that the agreement be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So it's correct, isn't it, that you're saying here that if the Bosnian Muslim side don't respect the agreement, then you would cut off power to Buca Potok. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, though, this never happened, and there were cases -- or there was situations when Grbavica did not have electricity and it was always a question of the cable breaking down, and I believe that. But I am saying, I'm telling you with full responsibility that we did not switch electricity off from Reljevo, even though I said that here. Perhaps we should have done that, though. But it's true that Grbavica would not receive electricity from Buca Potok, but we would never cut the electricity to the inner centre of town because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30732 receives number P6556, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, if the Bosnian Serb army wished to obstruct the flow of electricity to Sarajevo, they were able to do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: The Serbian army, if they wanted to cut the electricity, all they had to do was to ask me. I was in charge of electricity and I was the only one who could cut electricity off. Rather, my dispatchers at the transformer stations, not the army. Only I could have done it. This was my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to another exhibit, 65 ter 30733. While it's coming up, Mr. Lubura I'll tell you it's a VRS Main Staff order that relates to the flow of electricity signed by Manojlo Milovanovic dated the 21st of May, 1994. Under the subheading "I hereby order," we read the following: "Do not make any changes in the sphere of civilian functioning in Sarajevo or anywhere else without my permission. Especially, do not obstruct the flow of water, electricity, or gas without my permission because otherwise this could be turned against us." Mr. Lubura, consistent with your answer this document shows that the VRS, and specifically the Main Staff, were able to make decisions about whether or not to supply electricity to Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: The Main Staff -- actually, this confirms my words. The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska never ordered such a thing. Perhaps some lower-ranking commanders did try something like that or lower-ranking authority organs. But the Main Staff certainly did not. Had the Main Staff wished to do that, it could then send this letter to the director general of Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska who would then in turn order me to cut electricity to the Muslim side in the region. Not to me. The Main Staff -- you have to respect hierarchy in a state. It was the Main Staff. They would send the letter to the director general, Dr. Milorad Skoko of the Elektroprivreda enterprise. He would in turn order me and I would order my dispatchers to cut the electricity to the Muslim side. However, I state with full responsibility that I would not have done something like that, even if I had received an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that document as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30733 receives number P6557, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, you've testified today and also in the Karadzic case that you were not involved in the process of gaining approval for access to repair locations. You testified in the Karadzic case that you "... had no connections to either of the armed forces." That's transcript page T31058. Mr. Lubura, you meant you had no connections to either the VRS or the ABiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I did not have connections. I was a civilian and I was responsible to the civilian authorities. I reported to the general board of the Republika Srpska Elektroprivreda. It's a civilian body. And the general manager was appointed by the government of the RS. I could only have been in some friendly relations with them, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: As regards your connection to political structures in Republika Srpska, in the Karadzic case you testified at transcript page 31060: "I was not interested in politics. I'm an electrical engineer. My only job was to maintain and fix electricity facilities that were in my area of expertise." Do you confirm that testimony, Mr. Lubura?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I do. I was never a member of any party after 1979 until today. I have no political engagements and I'm no member of any party. From 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lubura, considering those two answers about your connections to the VRS and the connections to the political structures within Republika Srpska, I'd like to refer to paragraph 14 of your new statement, P501. We'll wait for a moment to get it onto our screens. Witness, in that paragraph 14 you state, and I quote: "I had the support of the highest political structures for my work, but also of the VRS, Army of Republika Srpska - Generals Mladic, Galic, and Milosevic - to make sure that everything that was needed to provide, transmit, and supply power to the whole of Sarajevo ... operated at the highest possible level. We were given approval for everything that it was possible to do, and we did it." Witness, this paragraph 14 in your new statement is quite a stretch from the position that you set out in the Karadzic case as regards your connection to political and military structures in Republika Srpska and their support for your work, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: May I explain? When fixing transmission lines which were in Serb territory but passing very close to Muslim lines, for example, the Visegrad-Rogatica and Sokolac transmission line, I had to go to military commands asking for security to be provided so that the Muslim side, from Zepa, for example, or from Gorazde, or from Ustipraca, so that they wouldn't arrive there and kill some of my workers. That is how they assisted me. That's what I meant. The VRS did assist me in the sense that they provided security for my teams carrying out repairs of transmission lines which were close to Muslim -- the Muslim lines. That is what I had in mind. As regards the political structures, sometimes independently and sometimes through the general board, I asked that uniforms and salaries and awards be provided for my workers who worked from 7.00 in the morning until 7.00 in the evening; that is to say, all day long. I did not have sufficient number of people who would install equipment. That was the support I enjoyed. The army also assisted me in the transport of equipment. For example, in Reljevo I had enormous quantities of conductors which needed to be sent to have lines built through the corridors. The army provided trucks. I didn't have ten or twenty, I only had one truck in my plant. That is how they did a service to me and assisted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: That is what this supplemental information --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you referred to the military commands that you would go to for security and the commands you would discuss transport with, did -- did those persons include Generals Mladic, Galic, and Milosevic? Were your questions specifically aimed at them?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I turned to -- directly to General Galic and General Milosevic. But I was present when they called General Mladic. He was the Chief of Staff so they had to obtain his approval, and of course they did. Of course they did. They explained why I needed ten trucks or a trailer to move the transformer and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Witness, on the basis of the support that was provided to you by the VRS for this security and the support for transport, that is the basis upon which you say that the -- the VRS did everything in their power to ensure electrical power to the whole area of Sarajevo operated at the highest level; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct. Precisely. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P358.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, this is coming up. It's an entry in the military notebook of General Mladic and it's dated the 5th of August, 1993, and it refers to a meeting held at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to e-court page 262 in the English and 260 in the B/C/S, please. Focus on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, we see this is a meeting held in Pale, Thursday, the 5th of August, 1993, meeting of the Supreme Command. Karadzic is noted as stating: [As read] "The European community has decided that the war in BH must end, but the US has not done that yet."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see on the third bullet that it states: "They will strike us if we don't do something." Number 1: "They have decided that we must withdraw from Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica. 2, "To have water, gas, and electricity brought to Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, we see now the minutes of a follow-up meeting with General Briquemont.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see Karadzic is quoted as stating: "We are prepared to hand over to the UN the positions of Mount Igman and Bjelasnica." And at number 2: "We are prepared to make possible regular supplies of water, gas, and electricity for Sarajevo." Mr. Lubura, these entries read together show that after pressure from the European community President Karadzic made a decision to "have water, gas, and electricity brought back to Sarajevo." Do you recall that decision?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I recall it well. Please. In 1993, the city of Sarajevo did have electricity just the way I explained. 20 plus 3. It also had water although I don't know what quantities. It was probably less due to failures. But it had electricity. The only thing that could happen is something I have already testified about previously; for example, if the Reljevo-Vogosca transmission line was interrupted or the other one going to Kiseljak, but that would last up to seven or eight days at the most. The city of Sarajevo did have electricity. The longest period it did not have electricity was between December 1992 until the 10th of January, 1993. The rest of the time Sarajevo did have electricity. Please. Mr. Karadzic probably knew there was electricity. The only time there was no electricity was when there were breakdowns. Only then. I claim responsibly again that no one ever ordered to me to cut electricity for Sarajevo. The Muslim side or the Serb side did not have electricity only when there were failures, when there were breakdowns. The agreement reached between myself and Durmic was honoured. I don't know. I mean, I don't know what Mr. Karadzic meant. Maybe he thought there should be more. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We'll stay on this topic and we'll stay on this decision that you recall well, but we'll go to another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter P02236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter or is it a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's a P number. Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P2236.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, this is a summary of an intercepted conversation recorded by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I do not know why it is under seal. Could you please keep that in mind when dealing with the document in open session, that even if the public doesn't see it from your questions, it may arise what the document is, and ... again, I have no --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll move on. I'll move on past this document. I'll move on [Indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can ask questions about it, but we might need to go into private session. That's -- I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mostly with these intercepts they are under seal because the location of the interceptors are secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, Your Honours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, still on the same topic --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Remaining on this topic, Mr. Lubura, I'd like to show you another document, P5205. And this is an agreement, a peace agreement signed by commanders of the warring parties dated the 11th of August, 1993. So that's -- that's the very next day after this -- after the document that we -- we've just looked at. On page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could see page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We read the undersigned -- at the top of the page, we read: "The undersigned military commanders as representatives of the parties in the conflict." And then in a couple of paragraphs later: "Hereby agree as follows."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to page 5 in the English, please. I think it's the same in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see article -- halfway down the page article 9, "Restoration of Infrastructure," "Principles for Restoration of Infrastructure."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is article 4, not 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry, forgive my incorrect interpretation of Roman numerals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: At 1B we see it states: "Interfering with the supply of water, gas, or electricity as a weapon or means of pressure is unacceptable. Infrastructure shall not be attacked or degraded in any way and shall not be used for any military purpose." If we go to the last page of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sorry, could we go a page back. And one more page back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, we see the signature there of General Mladic. Witness, it's correct, isn't it, that a couple of days after this peace agreement was signed electricity to the city of Sarajevo was turned back on?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I think this agreement was in force for all of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, and yet you seem to be applying it only to the region of Sarajevo. Sarajevo did have electricity. I say it yet again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. Could you please respond to the question, Witness. The question was whether -- or whether it's true that a couple of days after this peace agreement was signed electricity to the city of Sarajevo was turned back on. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even know that the electricity had been cut before the agreement was signed, Mr. President. Thus, I don't know whether it was turned back on after the signing. I don't know that. All I'm saying is that the only time when there was no electricity was when there was a technical malfunction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, I'd like to show you a final document in connection with this particular area we've been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter 30742, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lubura, while this is coming up, I'll tell you that it's an excerpt from a 1993 annual report by the public enterprise Elektroprivreda BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page of this document, which is page 10 of a larger exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness in the -- about halfway down the page, we read: "During 1993 the city was without electricity supply about 140 days. The longest cutout period occurred from June 21st to August 13 (53 days)." Mr. Lubura, this document shows that two days after General Mladic signed this peace agreement that prohibited the interference of -- with electricity as a means of pressure, that electricity to Sarajevo was turned back on; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: This BH Elektroprivreda document is something that I don't know if it is correct or not. But what they're saying, that there were 53 days in a single stretch when there was no electricity, I disagree. I'm positive it was not the case. Now, where they find these 53 days between June 21 and August 13, I don't know. I sincerely doubt it. I cannot recall all -- all such details. It was a long time ago. As far as I remember, there would be seven, eight, up to ten days at the most when there was major repair work to be done. I really don't remember any such long periods. And they're saying that for 140 days they were out of electricity? I could check that because there are log-books in the Republika Srpska Elektroprivreda where consumption is shown and when there was no electricity because each plant had its own log-book. For example, the one at the Reljevo transformer station. You can find there the time when there was no electricity, even if it was only for half an hour. I really don't know this document, and I have nothing to say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document as the next Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30742 receives number P6558, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. It's -- 6558 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. Before we take the break, I'd like to take the witness back for a second to P6554, but not to be shown at this moment. What I'd like to have on the screen is D502. And I add to that, that to the extent it is unclear in the transcript that P6554 was admitted, P6554 is admitted. If it's not clear yet, then it should be clear now. Could we have a look at D502. Witness, in that document I just referred to and where parts were read to you, there something was said about the Kosevo-Velesici line which you say is for the 100 per cent on the Muslim side. Could you -- and perhaps the usher could assist and give the witness a marker. Could you please mark exactly what you understand to be the Kosevo-Velesici line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That, then, apparently is a line which is not represented on this map. You now add to that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are cable lines, that's why they're not shown. These are aerial lines, above ground transmission lines. All these transformer stations were interconnected by cables. That's why I'm saying this document is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, why would you need a mixed -- a mixed team to make any repairs there? It sounds a bit ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At Kosevo-Velesici, a mixed team was not needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then have a look again at P6554, page --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. I think there is translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- I don't want to pose the question, but Mr. Lubura explained what kind of lines were presented on -- on this map and what kind of line was this green one. So I think it's not correctly presented in -- in the transcript and in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you again, then, explain what kind of line the green line is you marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are cable connections between Kosevo and Velesici. That's why I understand this reference. It's not on the territory of Republika Srpska at all. It's inside the city. Kosevo is connected by cable to Velesici, whereas these black lines -- Velesici are connected with, as you see, with Sarajevo 4 and Sarajevo 10, and that's an above ground connection going partly through Serb territory and partly through Muslim territory. Kosevo is connected with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- both number 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand you. First of all, the marking seems to have disappeared but perhaps was not saved. It's saved. Okay. Then, could -- first of all, could that receive a new number so that we -- that would then be a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a -- Mr. Lukic, would you mind if the little green extra line would be on your account?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a D number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document as marked by the witness receives number D507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If -- if we look at the document where it is discussed, it reads: "The repair has not been performed yet. The representative of Sector Sarajevo said that BH side had accepted to have a mixed team for the repair and that all necessary authorisation had been obtained, but a local BS commander had not aloud the team to do the repair on the 22nd of February." And then the Bosnian Serb side said that they would check with their authorities what was the problem. Now, what you would expect if we listen to your testimony is that the Bosnian Serb side would have said, What have we got to do with this totally internal BiH matter? We are not in any way involved in that. So if the BS side would check with their authorities and that the mission should be performed in a week, then that's difficult to reconcile with your answer that the Bosnian Serb side had got nothing to do with this repair, irrespective of whether there may be an unclear description of what line it exactly is about. Any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This must be an error. Transformer stations Kosevo and Velesici were connected by cable, not by above ground transmission lines. I don't know how Serbs could have contested it. Cables run underground. They are not above ground. And it runs through Muslim territory, 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have understood your earlier explanation. You say, I have no explanation for the position taken by the Bosnian Serb side during this meeting. Either it's reflected incorrectly or it is incomprehensible. We leave it to that. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. You follow the usher and be back after the break. Mr. Lukic, could you give us an indication as to how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Couple of minutes, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, a couple of minutes. Then we'll -- the only question which then remains, whether the next witness should remain standby because we resume at 2.00, five minutes past 2.00 for a couple of minutes ... Perhaps if the witness would remain standby. If there's ten minutes, then we still would use that. We take a break and we'll resume at 2.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, Mr. Lukic, we -- we agreed that the map marked again now with a green line would receive a D number - D507 - but I had not yet pronounced the words that it is admitted into evidence. It hereby is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just want to inform Your Honours and the witness that all my additional questions have already been answered, so I have nothing additional for this witness and I just want to thank him for answering to our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that doesn't trigger think any need for further question, Mr. Jeremy. Since the Bench has no further questions for you either, Mr. Lubura, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and having answered questions that were put to you by the parties and put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Usher, if you could please bring the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because, Mr. Traldi, you just had started your cross-examination for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cvoro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll be with us only for a very short time today. Unfortunately, we have not much time left, but I can assure you that tomorrow we'll spend far more time with you than we do today, which will not be more than ten minutes most likely. Could I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Cvoro.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, in our limited time today, I just want to ask you some basic questions about the makeup of Pale municipality during your time in office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 02559A. And if we could turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Looking at the left side of the screen, do you see the word "Pale" about a quarter of the way down the page?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the villages listed beneath it are villages that were in Pale municipality in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just glancing at it, yes. These are villages that belonged to Pale municipality. But if you want a more detailed answer, I would have to read it all. But just at a glance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then directing your attention to the far right side of the page, do you see the Italic number 10 across from Pale? Just continuing from Pale to the numbers to the far right side of the page.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see only one number, whether it's 10 or 20, I don't know. I think it's 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we then turn to the next page, page 3 in the B/C/S. And if we could zoom in on the same spot in the page, row number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this covers a period of several decades, but beginning on the left side we see figures for Pale in 1991, figures of 16.355 total persons with a 129 Croats, 4.364 Muslims, and 11.284 Serbs. That would make the municipality about 69 per cent Serb, 27 per cent Muslim, and 1 per cent Croat. Does that roughly accord with your recollection of the ethnic representation in Pale at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the beginning, when I became president of the Executive Board on the 1st of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I tendered 65 ter 02559A as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02559A receives number P6559, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6559 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask that we have 65 ter 30713 on our screens. This is an ethnic majority map of the Sarajevo area, including Pale. And I'd ask that we zoom in on the Pale municipality, just in the centre right part of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could take a minute to familiarise yourself with the depiction of villages on this map, and then let us know when you've done so.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The villages represented with blue dots had majority Serb populations before the war, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I'm not sure about Praca but Podgradac and the other villages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the villages coloured green had Muslim majorities before the war, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in the south-east corner we see a cluster of villages represented with green dots. Do you see those? Just to the east of Praca.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: On Friday at transcript page 21930, you mentioned a Muslim municipality called Pale Praca was established much later. Is it your evidence that this was the area where that Muslim municipality was eventually established?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's part of local commune Praca. I don't see Renovica here, but Renovica -- I'm not sure whether it was a local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That answers the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I can't see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd tendered 65 ter 30713 as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30713 receives number P6560, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, the witness expressed some doubts as to whether Praca was majority Serb. Now at least in one of the statistics, it's -- I think it gives 490 -- yes -- no, no, it's okay. Yes. Please proceed. It's -- it comes close. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it's represented on page four of this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was looking at that, and we have close to 500 Muslims to close to 600 Serbs. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn now to the assistance that the municipal authorities provided to some other Bosnian Serb institutions in Pale. The Defence showed you a report from the SRNA News Agency on Friday, and I suspect this will be the only institution I ask you about today. The director of SRNA was Todor Dutina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In April 1992, he came to see you and requested assistance in establishing the agency; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Move to channel 6 and see. Do you now receive translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In April 1992, Mr. Dutina came to see you and requested assistance in establishing SRNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you provided him with supplies, including a telephone with a telefax, a telephone number, and a typewriter, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And premises. Premises for the agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, sir. Now while you provided assistance, SRNA was established and founded by Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could just have 65 ter 16161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will be the last document we look at, Mr. Traldi, for today, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just directing your attention to article 1, it reads: "In order to meet the informative interests of the Serb people in BiH, we are forming public company Serb News Agency, SRNA." Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO CVORO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 16161 as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 16161 receives number P6561, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6561 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think that's a convenient time, Mr. President, to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Mr. Cvoro, we will already adjourn. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom. I instruct you as I did last Thursday, that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 4th of June, in this same courtroom, I, at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of June, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.19 p.m.,
